patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Burundian and Gabonese peacekeepers in the Central African Republic (2016): Not charged (per Wikipedia citing UN/AP)
patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In 2013 the Vatican recalled its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, while Dominican authorities were investigating him for abusing children, and later told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow him to be extradited. In 2020 a court in Seoul refused a US request to extradite Son Jong-woo, who had run the abuse website Welcome to Video. In 2013 Morocco's king pardoned Daniel Galván, a Spanish man convicted of raping children, as a gesture towards Spain. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

patterns.pattern: Peacekeepers and aid workers in crisis zones
patterns.role: Home country of accused troops or staff
patterns.role_note: Burundi → CAR: MINUSCA contingent allegations (offenders).
patterns.pattern_summary: In war zones and refugee camps, children have been sexually abused by soldiers and aid workers sent to protect them or to provide food and shelter. In 2002 a report by the UN refugee agency and Save the Children described aid workers and peacekeepers in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone trading food and other aid for sex with children. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that Sri Lankan peacekeepers had abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007, and 114 soldiers were sent home; none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In the Central African Republic, children reported abuse by French soldiers and UN troops in 2014 and 2015; French judges closed the case against the French soldiers in 2018 without charges. An independent commission found 83 alleged perpetrators among people working on the World Health Organization's Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo between 2018 and 2020, 21 of them WHO staff, and victims as young as 13. The UN has published yearly counts of these allegations against peacekeepers since 2004.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: Almost no reports reach the international systems
patterns.role_note: NCMEC 2025: 1,028 reports for Burundi
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: MINUSCA Burundian and Gabonese contingents — Dékoa allegations
cases.who: UN Multidimensional Integrated Stabilization Mission in CAR (MINUSCA) military contingents from Burundi and Gabon
cases.what: The Secretary-General's 2017 report states that two allegations recorded in MINUSCA, concerning incidents in Dékoa and military personnel from Gabon and Burundi, led to interviews of some 136 alleged victims and accounted for 48% of all victims recorded in 2016. Investigations by the troop-contributing countries were still pending. Press accounts reported that at least 98 girls described abuse and 41 troops were identified and sent home without charges.

cases.title: UN — Zeid report: 45% of 2004 peacekeeping SEA allegations involved sex with under-18s (2005)
cases.who: UN peacekeeping military and civilian personnel
cases.what: On 24 March 2005 the Secretary-General transmitted the report of his adviser Prince Zeid Ra'ad Zeid Al-Hussein on sexual exploitation and abuse in UN peacekeeping. Of 105 allegations recorded across missions in 2004, about 45% involved sex with persons under 18; in MONUC (DR Congo) 72 allegations were received between May and September 2004, and women interviewed described 'rape disguised as prostitution', with sex often costing about $1 to $3. OIOS considered 7 of the MONUC cases it examined fully substantiated and found convincing evidence in 2 more. The report recommended binding standards for all personnel, a professional investigative capacity, on-site courts martial and DNA paternity testing.

cases.title: AMISOM bases, Mogadishu — rape and sexual exploitation (HRW 2014)
cases.who: African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM) Ugandan and Burundian contingents
cases.what: Human Rights Watch's report of 8 September 2014, based on 50 interviews including 21 survivors, documented 10 incidents of sexual abuse, including rape and sexual assault, and 14 cases of sexual exploitation by African Union (AMISOM) soldiers, mainly Ugandan personnel at and around AMISOM's headquarters and Burundian personnel at their base in Mogadishu. Four rape cases and one sexual assault involved girls under 18; the youngest was a 12-year-old allegedly raped by a Ugandan soldier near Baidoa in May 2013. Many victims had gone to the bases to seek medicine or aid, including a woman seeking medicine for her sick baby, and interpreters facilitated soldiers' access; some women and girls were compelled into sex in exchange for money, food and medicine.

flows.what: UN data list allegations against Burundian contingent personnel involving 46 children.

networks.name: UN peacekeeping operations (Department of Peace Operations)
networks.what: UN Secretary-General reports record 357 SEA allegations against peacekeeping personnel in 2006, falling to 51 in 2014 and rising to 102 in 2024. In 2024, 27 of 125 identified victims were children. Most allegations since 2018 come from MONUSCO (DRC) and MINUSCA (CAR). Criminal accountability rests with troop-contributing countries; the UN can only repatriate.

networks.name: African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM)
networks.what: AU peace operation in Somalia. HRW in 2014 documented rape and sexual exploitation of women and girls as young as 12 on Mogadishu bases by Ugandan and Burundian soldiers.

patterns.pattern: Children taken by governments, then abused or given false identities
patterns.role: Dictatorship or occupation: children given to other families under false identities
patterns.role_note: Nazi Germany — kidnapping of Polish and other children for Germanization (RuSHA trial) (receiving or involved).
patterns.pattern_summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. By July 2025 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo had identified 140 of those children. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015, and by the end of 2014 nearly 38,000 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse at the schools. A US federal report in 2022 said many children at its 417 boarding schools suffered physical, sexual and emotional abuse. Britain sent children abroad to Australia, Canada and other countries under child migration schemes, and a 2018 inquiry found evidence that children sent under these schemes were sexually abused. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role: Where children are abused for paying viewers
patterns.role_note: Buyers → Regpay, Minsk (via Latvian banks).
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, found most of the material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports of suspected abuse to the US CyberTipline, most of them made by American technology companies, rose from 4,560 in 1998 to more than 36 million in 2023, then fell to about 20.5 million in 2024; the centre that runs it attributed part of the fall to Meta encrypting its messages. Money for watching abuse streamed live flows from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

cases.title: Nazi Germany — kidnapping of Polish and other children for Germanization (RuSHA trial)
cases.who: SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA), Lebensborn e.V., SS
cases.what: Nazi Germany seized children judged 'racially valuable' in occupied Poland and elsewhere, held them in Lebensborn and other homes and placed them with German families under new identities; DW reports estimates of up to 200,000 Polish children kidnapped and forcibly 'Germanized'. In the RuSHA trial (United States v. Ulrich Greifelt et al., Nuremberg Military Tribunal I), 14 leading officials of the SS Race and Settlement Main Office, Lebensborn and related bodies were charged with crimes including the kidnapping of 'racially valuable' children; charges were read on 10 October 1947, the trial ran from 20 October 1947 to 17 February 1948, and on 10 March 1948 the tribunal convicted 13 — Greifelt was sentenced to life — and acquitted one.

cases.title: Regpay — Minsk-based paid abuse sites / Operation Falcon
cases.who: Regpay Co. Ltd (Belarus) with Florida payment firm Connections
cases.what: Regpay Co. Ltd of Minsk, Belarus, processed paid memberships to about 50 websites, including child abuse sites it operated itself, serving thousands of subscribers worldwide; payments were laundered with help from Connections USA of Fort Lauderdale, Florida. US Attorney General John Ashcroft announced the case in January 2004 as part of Operation Falcon. Regpay's president Yahor Zalatarou and marketing director Alexei Buchnev were arrested at a Paris hotel on 30 July 2003 after a ruse by US agents, and technical administrator Aliaksandr Boika was arrested in Tarragona, Spain, on 31 July 2003 and extradited. All pleaded guilty in New Jersey. Buchnev was sentenced to 40 months in May 2006; Zalatarou and Boika were each sentenced to 25 years on 9 August 2006. Connections' chief executive pleaded guilty to money laundering. Hundreds of subscribers were arrested in the US and other countries.

flows.title: Buyers → Regpay, Minsk (via Latvian banks)
flows.what: Credit card payments for access to about 50 abuse websites run from Minsk were routed through Latvian banks; Florida firm Connections laundered money.

networks.name: SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA) and Lebensborn e.V.
networks.what: RuSHA racially screened children in occupied territories and Lebensborn ran camps and homes from which selected children were placed with German families under new identities. The Nuremberg RuSHA trial (1947–48) ruled the kidnapping and Germanization of children part of genocide.

networks.name: Russian state system for transfer, adoption and 're-education' of Ukrainian children
networks.what: ICC arrest warrants (17 March 2023) for Vladimir Putin and Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova for unlawful deportation and transfer of children. Yale HRL identified at least 43 camps in Russia and Crimea where at least 6,000 Ukrainian children were held in 2022. Ukraine counts 20,651 deported and/or forcibly displaced children and 2,752 returned (Oct 2026).

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 100,893 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman). 2005: scandal: Hunan orphanages found buying trafficked babies; 23 officials fired, traffickers jailed 2024: end: China ends intercountry adoption except by blood relatives / stepchildren (5 September)
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: China — Hunan orphanages bought trafficked babies for adoption (2005 convictions); China — intercountry adoption programme ended (2024) after trafficking cases.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 275 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: China — Hunan orphanages bought trafficked babies for adoption (2005 convictions)
cases.who: Six state orphanages in Hunan; traffickers from Guangdong; local officials
cases.what: Six Hunan orphanages were found buying infants from traffickers who brought them from Guangdong, placing nearly 1,000 children with domestic and foreign families between 2002 and 2005. In 2005, according to Xinhua, 23 civil officials were fired; three traffickers were sentenced to 15 years and six others to 3–13 years.

cases.title: Norway — NOU 2026:7 finds illegal and unethical intercountry adoptions
cases.who: Norwegian adoption organisations; Norwegian authorities; partner orphanages and bodies in 12 countries
cases.what: A government committee appointed in 2023 presented NOU 2026:7 'Forsvarlighet, risiko og tillit' on 22 June 2026. Examining adoptions from 12 countries since the 1950s, it concluded there were illegal or unethical conditions and that the Norwegian adoption system had clear shortcomings throughout the period. Individual findings included a kidnapped child adopted to Norway, a mother told she would get money if she consented, and documents deliberately falsified; payments to orphanages or organisations were sometimes linked to the number of children adopted.
cases.cover_up: Organisations did not always tell Norwegian authorities about payments or errors; authorities kept approving adoptions after learning of risks and illegalities.

cases.title: China — intercountry adoption programme ended (2024) after trafficking cases
cases.who: China Center for Children's Welfare and Adoption; state orphanages
cases.what: China opened intercountry adoption in 1992; about 160,000 children were sent abroad, peaking at almost 8,000 to the US in 2005. The programme came to depend increasingly on abuse, abduction and trafficking (New Yorker), including Hunan orphanages buying trafficked babies (2005). On 5 September 2024 the foreign ministry announced the end of the programme, except adoption by blood relatives or of a stepchild.

cases.title: Myanmar → China — Kachin women and girls sold as 'brides' (HRW 2019)
cases.who: Traffickers including relatives and acquaintances; buying families in China
cases.what: Human Rights Watch's 112-page report of 21 March 2019 documented women and girls from Kachin and northern Shan States, many displaced by conflict, sold for US$3,000–13,000 to Chinese families, locked up and raped so they would become pregnant. One survivor was trafficked at 16 by her sister-in-law. The 2025 US TIP report says displaced women and girls in Kachin and Shan remain vulnerable to forced marriage and forced childbearing in China.
cases.cover_up: HRW said Myanmar and Chinese authorities were 'looking away'; police on both sides gave traffickers little reason to fear enforcement.

cases.title: Vietnam and Laos → China — girls sold as brides (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers and marriage brokers
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP reports say traffickers in Vietnamese border villages lure women and girls, particularly Hmong, to China for forced marriages involving sex trafficking or forced labour, and use 'bride kidnapping' to exploit ethnic-minority girls in the northwest highlands; in Laos, traffickers increasingly kidnap or recruit women and girls via marriage brokers to China for sex trafficking, forced labour and forced surrogacy. Vietnam identified 236 child victims in 2024.

cases.title: Mongolia — girls sex-trafficked in Ulaanbaatar hotels and karaoke bars (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers in hotels, massage parlours, karaoke clubs
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says women and girls are sex-trafficked in Mongolian hotels, massage parlours, illegal brothels, bars and karaoke clubs, mostly in Ulaanbaatar, provincial centres and border areas, sometimes facilitated by a lack of police enforcement; traffickers use online platforms to groom and blackmail children; and children taken abroad for competitions have instead been put to work, e.g. as horse jockeys.
cases.cover_up: The report says exploitation is sometimes facilitated by lack of police enforcement; some families are complicit.

cases.title: Pakistan → China — 629 girls and women sold as 'brides' (AP 2019)
cases.who: Brokers selling poor (often Christian) Pakistani girls and women to Chinese men
cases.what: AP obtained a list compiled by Pakistan's Federal Investigation Agency of 629 girls and women sold as brides to Chinese men from 2018 to mid-2019. In October 2019 a court in Faisalabad acquitted 31 Chinese nationals charged in the biggest case. The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers target impoverished Christian communities to send women and girls to China, where hundreds reported being forced into commercial sex.
cases.cover_up: Officials told AP the investigation largely stopped after June 2019 because of pressure from government officials fearful of harming ties with Beijing; in October 2019 a Faisalabad court acquitted 31 Chinese nationals after witnesses were threatened or bribed into silence.

flows.title: China → United States
flows.what: US immigrant visas issued to children adopted from China, FY1994–FY2014 (peak 7,906 in FY2005).

flows.title: China → United States
flows.what: China sent about 160,000 children abroad for adoption from 1992 until it ended the programme on 5 September 2024; others went to Spain, Canada, the UK, the Netherlands, France and Australia.

flows.title: Pakistan → China ('bride' trafficking)
flows.what: Brokers sold poor Pakistani girls and women, many Christian, to Chinese men as brides.

flows.title: Kachin State, Myanmar → Yunnan and beyond, China ('bride' trafficking)
flows.what: Women and girls sold for $3,000–13,000 to Chinese families.

flows.title: Northern Vietnam → China (forced marriage)
flows.what: Hmong and other ethnic-minority women and girls lured or abducted to China for forced marriage.

flows.title: Laos → China (forced marriage, surrogacy)
flows.what: Lao women and girls kidnapped or recruited via marriage brokers to China.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: Czech Republic — Fr František Merta.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

cases.title: Welcome to Video — darknet CSAM site run from South Korea
cases.who: Welcome to Video (operator Son Jong-woo / Son Jung-woo)
cases.what: A Korean-run darknet site that sold access to child sexual abuse videos for Bitcoin; it held over 250,000 unique videos and its server had more than one million Bitcoin addresses, one per account. IRS-CI tracing of Bitcoin transactions located the server in South Korea, and the operator, Son Jong-woo, was arrested on 5 March 2018. On 16 October 2019 the US DOJ announced 337 users arrested and charged, with leads sent to 38 countries (Korean police counted 310 arrests in 32 countries, 223 of them Koreans). He served 18 months in South Korea; on 6 July 2020 the Seoul High Court refused US extradition, and in July 2022 he received a further 24 months for concealing proceeds. DOJ said 45% of the videos analysed had not been known before.
cases.cover_up: South Korean courts gave the operator 18 months on appeal (May 2019); Seoul High Court refused US extradition on 6 July 2020.

cases.title: Czech Republic — Fr František Merta
cases.who: Archdiocese of Olomouc; Archbishop Jan Graubner (alleged failure to report)
cases.what: In 2000–2001 Fr František Merta was found guilty of abusing more than 20 boys and received a two-year suspended sentence. Archbishop Jan Graubner allegedly failed to report him and moved him between parishes when problems arose.
cases.cover_up: Archbishop Graubner allegedly did not report him and moved him between parishes

cases.title: New Zealand DIA-led operation: 146 children safeguarded
cases.who: Tens of thousands of accounts sharing abuse material on an online service
cases.what: Begun in 2019 after an online service provider reported offenders exchanging imagery of the sadistic abuse of infants and children. By March 2022 it had opened 836 cases internationally, led to 46 arrests across New Zealand, identified more than 100 suspects in the EU and safeguarded 146 children; in Austria and Hungary suspects were abusing their own children.

cases.title: Operation Atelier — network of abuse photographers
cases.who: Professional photographers producing abuse material
cases.what: Czech-initiated and supported by Europol and Eurojust: a Czech photographer exploited socially and financially disadvantaged children (close to 70) and, with a Swedish partner, distributed images to customers in the EU and Canada. In 2014 ten people were arrested in the Czech Republic (5), Sweden (2), France, Ireland and Spain; 30 TB of data were seized.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

cases.title: Norway-led crypto-tracing operation: 28 arrests (2026)
cases.who: Buyers paying cryptocurrency for dark web forum access
cases.what: From late May to mid-June 2026 police in Canada, Czechia, Germany, Norway, Poland, Sweden and Switzerland arrested 28 men aged 22–54 suspected of paying cryptocurrency to access dark web forums with abuse videos; one used AI to generate material and some victims were family members. Norwegian police used a crypto-tracing method developed in 2025, which also identified two sellers.

cases.title: Operation Cumberland — AI-generated abuse material platform
cases.who: Paid platform distributing AI-generated abuse material (Danish main suspect)
cases.what: A Danish national arrested in November 2024 ran a platform distributing AI-generated abuse material he produced; users paid a symbolic fee for a password. Most arrests came on 26 February 2025 in an operation led by Danish police with 18 other countries; 273 suspects were identified and 25 arrested. Europol called it one of the first cases involving AI-generated CSAM and noted the lack of national laws covering it.

flows.what: A Czech photographer and Swedish partner distributed images of about 70 children to customers abroad.

The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

cases.title: Tbilisi photo studio producing abuse material for foreign buyers
cases.who: Photo studio owners and foreign clients
cases.what: Georgian police, with Australian and US authorities and Europol, arrested 11 members of a group including studio owners and American and Australian citizens who arranged the production of sexual images of girls aged 8 to 14 in rented apartments in Tbilisi. Some girls were abused with parental consent in exchange for 500–3,000 GEL (about €150–900).

flows.title: US and Australian buyers commission abuse material in Tbilisi
flows.what: American and Australian citizens were among 11 arrested for arranging production of sexual images of girls in Tbilisi.

networks.name: Kidflix
networks.what: Paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users (2022–2025), 91,000 videos; 1,393 suspects identified, 79 arrested.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2009: Guatemala — Dirección de los Archivos de la Paz (SEPAZ), 'Las adopciones y los derechos humanos de la niñez guatemalteca, 1977-1989' (2009).

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 24,212 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman). 2007: scandal + law: Casa Quivira raid (August, 46 children); Hague-compliant adoption law passed 11 December 2007 2008: closure: Guatemala stops new adoptions to the US from 1 January; US State Dept (9 January) says no new US adoptions until Hague-compliant 2010: report: CICIG report on illegal adoption finds 78% of 153 cases studied violated the law

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Guatemala — notary-run adoption trade to the US (1996–2007); Hogar Seguro Virgen de la Asunción — abuse, trafficking alerts and fire killing 41 girls; Guatemala — Peace Archives report: army and state role in adoptions of children during the war (1977–1989).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 275 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Hogar Seguro Virgen de la Asunción — abuse, trafficking alerts and fire killing 41 girls
cases.who: State-run children's home under the Secretariat of Social Welfare (SBS); National Civil Police
cases.what: About 700 children lived at the state home, built for a maximum of 500; most had committed no crime. Months before the fire prosecutors had recommended closing it over abuse allegations, and girls had protested overcrowding and alleged sexual abuse by staff. After an escape on 7 March 2017, police returned a group of girls and locked them in a room; on 8 March one girl set a mattress alight, killing 41 girls and injuring 15. The social welfare secretary, his deputy and the home's director were sacked and later charged. On 12 Aug 2025 a judge convicted six former officials of offences from manslaughter to abuse of authority, with sentences of 6 to 25 years; former secretary Carlos Rodas received 25 years and a police officer who held the key 13 years. The judge said the fire was the culmination of reported abuses not acted on, and ordered an investigation of former President Jimmy Morales.
cases.cover_up: Officials ignored repeated complaints: in November 2016 the Human Rights Ombudsman asked the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights for precautionary measures citing mistreatment and a trafficking network recruiting children from the home. On the day of the fire police guarding the locked room did not let the girls out.

cases.title: Lev Tahor — leaders convicted of kidnapping children
cases.who: Lev Tahor (ultra-Orthodox sect)
cases.what: In December 2018 Lev Tahor leaders Nachman Helbrans and Mayer Rosner took a 14-year-old girl and her 12-year-old brother in the night from their mother's home in upstate New York and moved them through several states to Mexico, where the girl was returned to the adult man the group had 'married' her to religiously at 13. The mother had fled the group's Guatemala compound in November 2018 and been granted sole custody. Both children were recovered in Mexico after three weeks. A federal jury convicted the two men in November 2021, and on 31 March 2022 each was sentenced to 12 years. Founder Shlomo Helbrans had been convicted in New York in 1994 of kidnapping a 13-year-old boy.

cases.title: Rendon-Reyes trafficking organization (Tenancingo)
cases.who: Rendon-Reyes Trafficking Organization, Tenancingo, Tlaxcala
cases.what: From December 2004 to November 2015 the Tenancingo-based Rendon-Reyes organization smuggled women and girls from Mexico and Central America into the US, forced them into prostitution and laundered proceeds back to Mexico. In January 2019 five members were sentenced in Brooklyn to between 15 and 25 years; others had pleaded guilty to racketeering and sex trafficking.

cases.title: Guatemala — Peace Archives report: army and state role in adoptions of children during the war (1977–1989)
cases.who: Guatemalan armed forces and National Police; Secretaría de Bienestar Social (Hogar Elisa Martínez); notaries and courts
cases.what: In September 2009 the Dirección de los Archivos de la Paz, part of the Peace Secretariat of the Presidency set up under President Álvaro Colom, published a study of adoptions during the internal armed conflict. It reviewed 333 of 670 adoption files recorded for 1977–1989 and found that the army and National Police transported children into the adoption system, that adoptions often rested on court declarations of abandonment with little effort to find parents, and that a 1977 decree let notaries formalise adoptions without a judge. Chief investigator Marco Tulio Álvarez told the press the children went mainly to the United States, Sweden, Italy and France.
cases.cover_up: Decree 54-77 (1977) let notaries complete adoptions without prior judicial approval; the welfare secretariat kept no record of how many children it received

cases.title: Guatemala — notary-run adoption trade to the US (1996–2007)
cases.who: Private notaries (notarios), baby brokers, foster homes, officials
cases.what: After the civil war ended in 1996, adoptions abroad rose each year, run almost entirely (about 98%) by private notaries who handled both sides without court review and charged $35,000 or more per child; 97% of children went to the US. CICIG's 2010 report studied 153 cases and found 78% violated the new law in some way. Guatemala passed a Hague-compliant law on 11 December 2007 and stopped new adoptions to the US from 1 January 2008; the US State Department announced on 9 January 2008 it would not allow new adoptions until procedures were compliant.

cases.title: Lev Tahor — Guatemala removal of 160 minors
cases.who: Lev Tahor
cases.what: In December 2024 Guatemalan authorities removed 160 minors from a Lev Tahor farm compound in Oratorio after abuse and trafficking complaints; in January 2025 Interpol arrested a member in Guatemala on trafficking charges. The group had earlier fled child-protection proceedings in Quebec (2013, where authorities sought care for 127 children) and Ontario.

cases.title: Guatemala — Casa Quivira raid: 46 children possibly stolen for adoption
cases.who: Casa Quivira private adoption home (run by a US citizen and his Guatemalan wife); two lawyers
cases.what: On 11 August 2007 Guatemalan police found 46 children aged a few days to three years at the Casa Quivira adoption home in Antigua after neighbours reported foreigners collecting children daily. Two lawyers who allegedly processed the adoptions were arrested. Attorney General Mario Gordillo said most of the children lacked proper documents and his office was investigating whether they had been stolen or obtained from mothers under coercion.

cases.title: Honduras, El Salvador, Guatemala — gangs exploit girls; North American offenders (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Gangs and criminal organizations; foreign offenders
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP reports say criminal organizations including gangs exploit girls in sex trafficking in urban Honduras and Guatemala, and that men from Canada and the US exploit Honduran children. In El Salvador, foreign tourists sexually exploit children and the rapid growth of tourism has created new risks; an estimated 140,000–200,000 Salvadoran children have a parent abroad or detained. Guatemalan children are exploited in Mexico and the US and in live-streamed abuse.

flows.title: Guatemala City → United States
flows.what: US immigrant visas issued to children adopted from Guatemala, FY1994–FY2014 (peak 4,728 in FY2007).

flows.title: Guatemala / Honduras → Mexico → United States (children in sex trafficking)
flows.what: Guatemalan and Honduran adults and children exploited in sex trafficking in Mexico, the US, Belize and El Salvador.

flows.title: Chatham-Kent, Ontario → Guatemala (Lev Tahor flees child-protection orders)
flows.what: After a Quebec court ordered 14 children into foster care in November 2013 and the group moved to Ontario, members with children left for Guatemala in 2014; nine who tried to flee via Trinidad and Tobago were returned to Canada.

networks.name: Tenancingo (Tlaxcala) pimping family networks
networks.what: Family-based pimping networks from Tenancingo, Tlaxcala, that recruited Mexican and Central American women and girls by deception and forced them into prostitution in New York and other US cities. Several were prosecuted in Brooklyn (Carreto family, 2005–2008; Rendon-Reyes organization, 2019).

networks.name: Lev Tahor
networks.what: Ultra-Orthodox sect of about 200–300 people founded in Israel in 1988 by Shlomo Helbrans, accused of child abuse and forced marriage of teenage girls. Leaders were convicted in the US in 2021 of kidnapping two children.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: Minnesota → India: Fr Joseph Jeyapaul (returned by extradition 2014).
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: Years of waiting: protected by status
patterns.role_note: Muzaffarpur shelter home: first report 2018, first action 2018 (0 years). Operator Brajesh Thakur was politically connected; TISS social audit (report April 2018) exposed abuse; minister Manju Verma resigned; CBI later cleared her despite call records showing contact with Thakur Asaram Bapu: first report 2013, first action 2013 (0 years). Witnesses were attacked: a former aide shot dead May 2014; key Surat witness shot dead January 2015 Unnao rape case (MLA Kuldeep Singh Sengar): first report 2017, first action 2018 (1 years). The victim's father died in police custody; arrest came only after the Allahabad High Court ordered it Bishop Franco Mulakkal (acquitted): first report 2018, first action 2018 (0 years). A nun's June 2018 complaint alleged 13 rapes 2014-2016; arrested only on 21 Sept 2018 after protests by nuns
patterns.pattern_summary: For 41 cases on this map the sources give two dates: the year a complaint first reached the police, a church, an employer or another official body, and the year someone was first charged, convicted or named in an official finding. The middle of those waits is 12 years. In Rochdale in 1968, a pupil told the police about the local politician Cyril Smith and was told that Smith was "a very important, powerful man". In 1970 Smith was assured he would not be prosecuted. In 2012, two years after his death, prosecutors said he should have been charged. Complaints about Jimmy Savile, one of the BBC's best-known presenters, reached the police from 1958, and he was never charged while he was alive. Gymnasts complained about the team doctor Larry Nassar from 1997, and he was first charged in 2016. The map colors each country by the longest wait among its cases.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Nithyananda: Fugitive
patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In 2013 the Vatican recalled its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, while Dominican authorities were investigating him for abusing children, and later told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow him to be extradited. In 2020 a court in Seoul refused a US request to extradite Son Jong-woo, who had run the abuse website Welcome to Video. In 2013 Morocco's king pardoned Daniel Galván, a Spanish man convicted of raping children, as a gesture towards Spain. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found South Asia lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation. Scholars note allegations "often remain informal and rarely progress to formal charges" (Matthew N. Schmalz)
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Muzaffarpur shelter home — TISS audit and convictions
cases.who: Sewa Sankalp Evam Vikas Samiti (state-funded NGO run by Brajesh Thakur); Bihar Social Welfare Department
cases.what: A social audit of Bihar shelter homes by the Tata Institute of Social Sciences, submitted in April 2018, flagged sexual abuse at the Muzaffarpur girls' home run by Brajesh Thakur's NGO; an FIR followed on 31 May 2018. Medical examination indicated sexual abuse of 34 girls, most of them children. The Supreme Court took up the case and, at the CBI's request, transferred the trial to a POCSO court at Saket, Delhi, because the accused were influential in Bihar. On 20 January 2020 that court convicted Thakur and 18 others; Thakur was sentenced to life imprisonment and has appealed.
cases.cover_up: The then district child protection officer was among the accused; Bihar Social Welfare Minister Manju Verma resigned over the case; the Supreme Court criticised the state for funding the NGO and moved the trial to Delhi. CBI cleared Verma and her husband, a finding disputed by The Caravan.

cases.title: Unnao rape case — MLA Kuldeep Singh Sengar
cases.who: Kuldeep Singh Sengar (BJP MLA, Uttar Pradesh)
cases.what: Sengar, then a BJP MLA in Uttar Pradesh, was convicted in December 2019 by a special CBI court in Delhi of raping a minor girl in Unnao district in 2017, and sentenced to life imprisonment; the BJP had expelled him. In December 2025 the Delhi High Court suspended his sentence; on 29 Dec 2025 the Supreme Court stayed that order on the CBI's appeal, and in May 2026 it set the suspension aside, directing the High Court to decide his appeal against conviction within three months or pass a fresh order.
cases.cover_up: The victim's father died in police custody; in July 2019 a truck crash killed two of her aunts and critically injured her and her lawyer (a court later accepted the CBI finding of no foul play in the crash). The arrest came only after the Allahabad High Court ordered it in 2018.

cases.title: India — Andhra Pradesh adoption racket (Tender Loving Care Home)
cases.who: St Teresa's Tender Loving Care Home and other agencies
cases.what: On 22 March 2001 Hyderabad police arrested a man carrying three baby girls allegedly bound for St Teresa's Tender Loving Care Home; other agencies were also flagged. A chargesheet said the home earned Rs 3.33 crore from intercountry adoptions, mainly to the US, in 1999–2001. On 31 August 2005 Sister Teresa Maria Kattikaran and nine others were sentenced to six months' imprisonment for cheating and forgery, and Andhra Pradesh became the first state to bar private agencies from placing children.

cases.title: Fr Joseph Jeyapaul — Indian priest extradited to Minnesota
cases.who: Diocese of Crookston, Minnesota; diocese in India
cases.what: An Indian priest serving in the Diocese of Crookston in 2004–2005 was removed from ministry in September 2005 and returned to India. He was charged in 2006 with raping a girl from age 14; extradition took about five years after an Interpol alert, with arrest in Erode, India in 2012 and return to Minnesota in November 2014. In 2015 he pleaded guilty to criminal sexual misconduct involving a teenage girl and was sentenced to a year and a day (time served); the rape charges were dismissed under the plea deal and he faced deportation to India.
cases.cover_up: The Vatican recommended his removal from the priesthood, but the Indian bishop instead imposed a year in a monastery through a canonical trial, and he continued as a priest in India.

cases.title: Devadasi dedication of girls — Karnataka and neighbouring states
cases.who: Temple dedication practice (mostly Dalit girls)
cases.what: Girls, mostly from Dalit families, are dedicated to temple deities and then sexually exploited, despite laws against the practice, including Karnataka's 1982 ban. The Karnataka government's last survey, in 2008, counted 40,600 devadasis; NGOs and a 2018 Karnataka State Women's University study found more than 80,000. Girls as young as seven have been pushed into the tradition.

cases.title: Nepal — National Human Rights Commission national reports on trafficking: an estimated 5,000 children trafficked in a year
cases.who: Trafficking networks moving women and girls across the open border to India and on to third countries
cases.what: Nepal's National Human Rights Commission, through its Office of the Special Rapporteur on Trafficking in Persons, has published national reports on trafficking since 2005. Its report released in August 2019 estimated that about 35,000 Nepalis were trafficked in 2018, including 5,000 children, and that nearly 1.5 million were at risk. It said nearly 1,000 Nepali women and girls are rescued from India each year and that poor screening at the open border makes cross-border trafficking hard to control. Its 2018 report said girls and women are trafficked to India for prostitution, orchestra dancing, circus work and marriage, and some are moved on to third countries.

cases.title: TISS 'Koshish' social audit of 110 Bihar children's homes
cases.who: Children's and girls' homes funded by the Bihar Social Welfare Department, many NGO-run
cases.what: At the Bihar government's request, the Koshish unit of the Tata Institute of Social Sciences visited 110 children's homes in 38 districts and submitted its audit to the Social Welfare Department on 27 April 2018, grading homes as better, administrative negligence or criminal negligence. The Muzaffarpur girls' home run by Sewa Sankalp Evam Vikas Samiti was graded criminal negligence, and the report raised harassment or abuse at 14 other homes, including a girls' home with complaints of severe sexual harassment and violence and homes where children were routinely beaten. The audit triggered the Muzaffarpur FIR of 31 May 2018 and later CBI cases against other Bihar shelter homes.
cases.cover_up: In the audited Bhagalpur home staff refused to give the audit team the key to the complaint box, saying it was lost; the department's director evaded questions about action on the other 14 homes.

cases.title: SOS Children's Villages — Independent Special Commission (ISC) worldwide report (2023)
cases.who: SOS Children's Villages (federation of member associations; International Senate); former senior staff
cases.what: An Independent Special Commission appointed by the International Senate of SOS Children's Villages in 2021, chaired by former Kenyan Chief Justice Willy Mutunga with former Delhi High Court acting chief justice Gita Mittal, issued its summary report on 6 June 2023. Using a 'reasonable grounds to believe' standard, it confirmed serious allegations of child sexual and physical abuse in several member associations in Africa, Asia and Central America, and found cover-ups of past sexual abuse and failures to report to national authorities in more than one association. Countries named in the report include Nepal, Cambodia, India, Kenya, Panama, Sierra Leone and Syria. A confidential 991-page part two went to the organisation's Senate and Executive Board on 2 May 2023; in November 2025 SOS Children's Villages International said it was examining whether parts could be passed to prosecutors.
cases.cover_up: Former senior staff in some member associations knew of abuse and failed to act or concealed reports; serious abuse was not reported to national authorities.

cases.title: Switzerland — authorities' irregularities in intercountry adoptions (Sri Lanka, India, Tibet…); proposed ban
cases.who: Swiss federal and cantonal authorities; private adoption agencies
cases.what: Swiss authorities soon realised that the placement of children for adoption, often wrongly presented as orphans, was also driven by economic interests and linked to organised child trafficking; decisions were often made on incomplete or falsified documents, and checks on foster families and on legal requirements were insufficient. From the 2010s, under pressure from groups such as Back to the Roots, intercountry adoptions from Tibet, Sri Lanka and India drew public attention. In 2018 the Federal Assembly commissioned a study on intercountry adoption; the Federal Council acknowledged the authorities' irregularities and omissions in 2020 and 2023, and at the end of 2024 recommended a general ban on intercountry adoption.

cases.title: ISKCON boarding schools (gurukulas) — acknowledged abuse
cases.who: International Society for Krishna Consciousness (ISKCON)
cases.what: In the 1990s ISKCON leaders acknowledged physical, emotional and sexual abuse of children in the movement's boarding schools in the US and India in the 1970s and 1980s, and in 1998 ISKCON itself published an exposé. A $900 million lawsuit filed in Texas in 2002 (the Turley case) led ISKCON temples into Chapter 11 bankruptcy and a $15 million settlement in 2008. ISKCON then set up a Child Protection Office.

cases.title: Deoria shelter home, Uttar Pradesh — girls rescued, CBI case
cases.who: Maa Vindhyavasini Mahila Prashikshan Evam Samaj Sewa Sansthan (NGO); director Girija Tripathi and superintendent Kanchan Lata Tripathi
cases.what: The case came to light when a 10-year-old girl escaped to a women's police station and said girls were taken away in cars in the afternoons and returned crying in the morning. Police rescued 24 girls on 5 August 2018 and sealed the home. Police charge-sheeted the director and her daughter, and seven others in a second FIR. In 2019 the CBI took over and registered cases including sexual harassment, human trafficking, sexual assault and adoption without legal procedure.
cases.cover_up: The UP Women and Child Development Minister said the NGO's recognition had been revoked and funds stopped a year earlier, yet it continued to operate; the government said it would examine who was responsible.

cases.title: Kolkata red-light areas — rescues of trafficked Nepali girls and minors (2015, 2025)
cases.who: Brothel keepers and traffickers in Kolkata
cases.what: In January 2015 police, with International Justice Mission and three NGOs, freed six young women trafficked from Nepal from four brothels in Kolkata's largest red-light area; all had fake adult ID documents, which IJM said traffickers issue to underage girls. On 10 September 2025 Kolkata Police's Anti-Human Trafficking Unit rescued ten people including nine minor girls from a house in Burtolla, North Kolkata, and arrested six people, including the couple running it (charged). The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers recruit significant numbers of Nepali and Bangladeshi women and girls for sex trafficking in India.

cases.title: India — Malaysian Social Services, Chennai: children kidnapped for adoption
cases.who: Malaysian Social Services adoption agency
cases.what: Police suspected the family running the Malaysian Social Services agency since 1991 of kidnapping and trafficking more than 350 children; in May 2005 Chennai police arrested three family members and six others. Children allegedly had their appearance changed and histories fabricated; officers found files for 120 children sent overseas. TIME reported in 2008 that Australian authorities had earlier warnings.

cases.title: India — Preet Mandir, Pune: CBI case on inter-country adoption racket
cases.who: Preet Mandir adoption agency; state officials
cases.what: Preet Mandir placed 518 children in 2004–2006, most abroad, and Frontline reported in 2005 it handled about 7% of India's foreign adoptions while charging high 'donation' fees. CNN-IBN reported in December 2007 that the CBI had confirmed findings on illegal adoptions. On 18 May 2010 the CBI registered a case against a managing trustee and state officials over an alleged inter-country adoption racket.

cases.title: 'Sweetie' sting — 20,000 offers to pay for webcam abuse
cases.who: Terre des hommes Netherlands (virtual 10-year-old 'Sweetie')
cases.what: In a 10-week investigation run from a warehouse in Amsterdam, Terre des hommes Netherlands posed in public chatrooms as 'Sweetie', a computer-generated 10-year-old Filipina girl, to show the scale of webcam child sex abuse: 20,000 internet users offered to pay for webcam sex performances. The researchers identified about 1,000 of them, from 65 countries, including 110 in the UK and 254 traced to computers in the US, and on 4 November 2013 handed their details to Interpol. They said online child exploitation had become a hardened criminal industry in the Philippines.

cases.title: Nepal → India — trafficking of girls to Indian brothels (estimates)
cases.who: Trafficking networks recruiting via false job, marriage and online romance offers
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers use job offers and online romance scams to recruit Nepali women and children to India for sex trafficking; Nepali courts convicted 406 traffickers (231 for sex trafficking) in the year. A 2024 study it cites found a majority of workers in Nepal's adult entertainment sector were sex-trafficking victims, nearly half of them children. Research collated on Wikipedia gives estimates of 5,000–10,000 Nepali women and girls trafficked to India each year across a 1,850 km open border.
cases.cover_up: US TIP 2025: serious concerns of official complicity; traffickers bribe some Indian officials to fly Nepali workers to third countries.

cases.title: Kamathipura, Mumbai — red-light district fed by trafficking from Nepal and Indian states
cases.who: Brothels of Kamathipura
cases.what: Kamathipura, Mumbai's oldest and largest red-light district and one of Asia's largest, was established over 150 years ago under British rule; the BBC in 2013 put its sex workers at an estimated 20,000. Girls were trafficked there from poor villages in other Indian states, some as young as 11, on promises of domestic work. The 2025 US Trafficking in Persons report is cited, though it could not be opened for this map, for a shift of sex trafficking in India toward spas, hotels and private residences, and for 2022 crime-data figures of 204 convicted traffickers and 1,134 acquittals; that report could not be opened in this pass (state.gov blocked).

cases.title: Bangladesh — girls trafficked to India, Pakistan and the Gulf; Rohingya girls near Cox's Bazar (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers, recruitment agents, armed groups in Rohingya camps
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit Bangladeshi women and girls in sex trafficking abroad, including in India, Pakistan and Gulf countries, and observers estimate children are 40 per cent of Bangladeshi sex-trafficking victims exploited abroad. Tourists have increased demand for sexual exploitation, including of Rohingya girls, near Cox's Bazar, where more than one million Rohingya refugees live in 33 camps. Courts convicted 103 traffickers, down from 407.
cases.cover_up: Corruption and official complicity were significant concerns; corrupt policing in Rohingya camps.

flows.what: Removed from ministry in Minnesota in 2005, he returned to India and continued as a priest; charged in 2006, he was arrested in Erode in 2012 and extradited back in 2014.

networks.what: Not one organisation: thousands of local traffickers, often parents or relatives, paid by foreign buyers to livestream abuse. IJM: 1 in 100 Filipino children affected in 2022.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. networks.name: Asaram Bapu ashrams
networks.what: Network of ashrams and gurukuls; founder Asaram convicted in 2018 of raping a 16-year-old and in 2023 in a Surat sisters' case. Two boys died at the Motera gurukul in 2008; an inquiry blamed ashram negligence.

networks.name: International Society for Krishna Consciousness (ISKCON)
networks.what: Acknowledged abuse in its boarding schools in the 1970s–80s; $15 million settlement in 2008.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2017: Independent Jersey Care Inquiry.
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Jersey care system and Haut de la Garenne — Independent Jersey Care Inquiry.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 275 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Jersey care system and Haut de la Garenne — Independent Jersey Care Inquiry
cases.who: States of Jersey children's services; Haut de la Garenne children's home
cases.what: The Independent Jersey Care Inquiry reported in July 2017 after hearing from about 450 people connected with Jersey's care system since 1945. It found the States of Jersey had been 'an ineffectual and neglectful substitute parent', that its child-welfare law was decades behind, and that some children in care might still be at risk. Haut de la Garenne, centre of the 2007–2010 police investigation Operation Rectangle, was described as a symbol of the turmoil and the inquiry recommended its buildings be demolished. Chief Minister Ian Gorst apologised: 'We failed children who needed our care.'
cases.cover_up: The inquiry found the authorities failed to build a culture of transparency, feeding perceptions of collusion and cover-up, and a 'small island culture' that was not countered.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found Middle East and North Africa lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Gulf states block Roblox over child safety (2025)
cases.who: Roblox Corporation
cases.what: In August 2025 Qatar blocked access to Roblox (13 August) and Kuwait's telecoms regulator temporarily blocked it (21 August) after parents and community groups raised child-safety concerns; Turkey had blocked it on 7 August. Roblox had been banned in Oman and Jordan since 2020, and was banned in the UAE from 2018 to 2021. Wikipedia additionally reports that Bahraini MPs drafted a ban, Palestine announced a ban in November 2025, Kazakhstan's and Kyrgyzstan's authorities warned parents about predators, and Buenos Aires and three Argentine provinces blocked it on school devices after grooming reports.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role: Hosts the most reported abuse material (IWF 2025)
patterns.role_note: 9,941 web addresses actioned by the IWF in 2025 (3% of the total).
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, found most of the material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports of suspected abuse to the US CyberTipline, most of them made by American technology companies, rose from 4,560 in 1998 to more than 36 million in 2023, then fell to about 20.5 million in 2024; the centre that runs it attributed part of the fall to Meta encrypting its messages. Money for watching abuse streamed live flows from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

cases.title: Boystown darknet platform
cases.who: Boystown (Tor platform, about 400,000 registered users)
cases.what: Boystown launched in June 2019, focused on the abuse of boys, and had 400,000 registered users when a BKA-led taskforce with Europol, the Netherlands, Sweden, Australia, Canada and the US took it down in April 2021. Three German administrators were arrested in Germany and one German national in Paraguay. In December 2022 they were sentenced to between 7 and 12 years, two with preventive detention. Successor platforms with a common German administrator were shut down around Christmas 2022.

cases.title: Moldova — children recruited online; institution leavers at risk (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers using social media and fake job ads
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers increasingly use social media and video chat to recruit children through fake job ads and exploit them in commercial sex, use abuse material as a grooming method, and target children in or leaving state institutions. Courts convicted 33 traffickers (22 for sex trafficking) in 2024.
cases.cover_up: A former police officer was convicted of labour trafficking (20 years); corruption and complicity remained significant concerns.

cases.title: Moldova — children leaving residential institutions targeted by traffickers
cases.who: Moldovan state residential institutions and boarding schools (Ministry of Education, Health, Labour)
cases.what: Moldova had 68 residential institutions for children in the mid-2000s; children left them at 15–16 with no support beyond about US$70 and no follow-up. UNICEF reported that research showed institutionalised children were several times more vulnerable to trafficking than other children and that 'they often become easy prey for traffickers'. The US State Department's March 2007 human rights report said women and children were trafficked for sexual exploitation to Russia, Turkey, Israel, the UAE and other countries, and that 12% of trafficking victims assisted by IOM were minors.

cases.title: Bosnia — trafficking of women and girls; IPTF monitors and SFOR/DynCorp contractors
cases.who: Traffickers and bar owners; local Bosnian police; UN International Police Task Force (IPTF) monitors; US SFOR civilian contractors (DynCorp)
cases.what: Human Rights Watch's November 2002 report 'Hopes Betrayed' documented women and girls trafficked mostly from Moldova, Romania and Ukraine into post-war Bosnia and held in debt bondage in bars and brothels. Local police were found acting as owners, guards and clients; 18 IPTF monitors who purchased women, visited brothels or faced trafficking-related charges went home, and none was confirmed prosecuted. A US Army CID report documented DynCorp contractors buying women from brothels; one confessed to buying a woman (with an Uzi) for 1,600 Deutschmarks. On 2 August 2002 a British employment tribunal unanimously found DynCorp had unfairly dismissed IPTF monitor Kathryn Bolkovac after she reported the trafficking.
cases.cover_up: Immunity: IPTF monitors were repatriated rather than prosecuted (18 returned home; HRW found no prosecution by Nov 2002); DynCorp contractors were sent home, preventing their use as witnesses; DynCorp fired whistleblower Kathryn Bolkovac in April 2001.

cases.title: Kosovo — trafficking for forced prostitution and the international presence (Amnesty 2004)
cases.who: Criminal networks; demand from NATO KFOR soldiers, UN police and international staff
cases.what: Amnesty International's May 2004 report said Kosovo had become a major destination for women and girls trafficked for forced prostitution since NATO troops and UN administrators arrived in 1999, with the international presence generating 80% of traffickers' income at the time. Women and girls were brought mainly from Moldova, Romania, Ukraine and Russia via Serbia, and local girls were also abducted. The UN peacekeeping department acknowledged in 2004 that peacekeepers had 'come to be seen as part of the problem in trafficking rather than the solution'.
cases.cover_up: Amnesty found no evidence of criminal proceedings against any military personnel in their home countries.

flows.title: Moldova → Russia, Turkey, Israel, UAE (trafficking of women and children, incl. institution leavers)
flows.what: The US State Department (March 2007) reported women and children trafficked from Moldova for sexual exploitation, increasingly to Russia and the Middle East including Turkey, Israel and the UAE; UNICEF found children leaving Moldova's residential institutions were several times more vulnerable to trafficking than other children.

flows.what: Women and girls mostly from Moldova, Romania and Ukraine sold to Bosnian bar owners; local police, IPTF monitors and US contractors implicated.

flows.title: Moldova/Romania/Ukraine/Russia → Kosovo via Serbia: trafficking
flows.what: Amnesty (2004): international presence generated 80% of income for traffickers.

cases.title: Mongolia — girls sex-trafficked in Ulaanbaatar hotels and karaoke bars (US TIP 2025)

cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says women and girls are sex-trafficked in Mongolian hotels, massage parlours, illegal brothels, bars and karaoke clubs, mostly in Ulaanbaatar, provincial centres and border areas, sometimes facilitated by a lack of police enforcement; traffickers use online platforms to groom and blackmail children; and children taken abroad for competitions have instead been put to work, e.g. as horse jockeys.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 2023: inquiry: Norway launches investigation into illegal or unethical intercountry adoptions
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Children taken by governments, then abused or given false identities
patterns.role: State-backed adoption systems that falsified children's papers
patterns.role_note: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses (receiving or involved).
patterns.pattern_summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. By July 2025 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo had identified 140 of those children. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015, and by the end of 2014 nearly 38,000 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse at the schools. A US federal report in 2022 said many children at its 417 boarding schools suffered physical, sexual and emotional abuse. Britain sent children abroad to Australia, Canada and other countries under child migration schemes, and a 2018 inquiry found evidence that children sent under these schemes were sexually abused. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.
